requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Take a tour of a library. Discuss with your counselor how the library is organized and what resources and/or services are offered in the library. (b) Learn how to search for material using a library's card catalog or computerized catalog by author, title, and subject. (c) In a library, search the card catalog or computerized catalog for six books of four different types, such as poetry, fiction, nonfiction, and biographies. (d) With the assistance of your counselor or the librarian, see if you can locate on the shelves the six books you selected. (e) Explain what a library card is, why it is needed, and how to get one.

requirements.lead_text: Read four different types of books, such as poetry, fiction, nonfiction, or biographies. Do one of the following for each book you have read:
requirements.req_text: Read four different types of books, such as poetry, fiction, nonfiction, or biographies. Do one of the following for each book you have read: (a) Write a review of the book. Include what you liked and/or didn't like about the book. Include whether you would recommend this book, and if so, who might enjoy reading it. (b) Watch a movie based on the book. What was the same between the book and movie? What was different? Which did you enjoy more? Discuss this with your counselor. (c) Give a book talk to your class, troop, or patrol.

pamphlet_excerpts: Requirement Asks Read: Requirement 3 asks you to read books of different types.
Books Aredivided Big: Books aredivided into two big groups depending on whether they are based onfacts or imagined stories.
There Types Genres: There are many types, or genres, of bookswithin these groups.
Genre Group Books: A genre is a group of books that share somethingin common.
step_by_step_procedure: Books Fantasy Genre: Books in the fantasy genre tell imaginedstories about places and circumstances that cannot be logically true.
Reader Expected Suspend: Yet the reader is expected to suspend disbelief, or go along with theauthor on this reading adventure.
Nonfiction Includes Factual: Nonfiction includes factual writing such as the Scouts BSA handbook, Fieldbook, merit badge pamphlets, and field guides.
Readnonfiction Information: You readnonfiction to get information or learn about a subject, person, or event.

requirements.lead_text: With your counselor's and parent or guardian's permission, choose ONE of the following activities and devote at least four hours of service to that activity. Discuss your participation with your counselor.
requirements.req_text: With your counselor's and parent or guardian's permission, choose ONE of the following activities and devote at least four hours of service to that activity. Discuss your participation with your counselor. (a) Read to a sick, blind, or homebound person in a hospital or in an extended-care facility. (b) Perform volunteer work at your school library or a public library. (c) Read stories to younger children, in a group or individually. (d) Organize a book swap in your troop, school, or place of worship. (e) Organize a book drive to collect books. Donate them to an organization in need.

pamphlet_excerpts: Talk Different Kinds: Talk with your counselor about the different kinds of volunteerservice you might give.
People Read Favorite: For many people, being read to is a favorite memory fromchildhood.
Chances Funthan They: Chances are, you’ll have even more funthan they will.
Reading Aloud Different: Reading aloud is a different skill from reading to yourself.
step_by_step_procedure: Losing Audience Read: To keep from losing your audience, you must read slowly.
Ifyou Normally Fast: Ifyou’re normally a fast talker, you may have to slow down yourreading so much that, to your own ears, at least, you sounddraggy.
They Follow Story: They will follow the story much better if you go slowly, sayevery word, read with enthusiasm, and insert a few pauses fordramatic effect.
Read Anaudience Listener: Before you read to anaudience (of one listener or many), practice the materialyou have chosen.

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers Center Reading: Careers that center around reading can be incredibly fulfilling for those who have apassion for books, literature, or gathering and interpreting.
Careersoften Involve Skills: Such careersoften involve skills like analysis, communication, and creative thinking.
Manyreading-focused Roles: Manyreading-focused roles allow individuals to immerse themselves in stories, ideas, oracademic research, making them ideal for lifelong learners.
Examples Careers Realm: Examples of careers in this realm include librarians, who manage collections ofbooks and digital resources while guiding others in their reading.
step_by_step_procedure: Editorsand Proofreaders Path: Editorsand proofreaders are another path; they play a critical role in refining written content for publication.
Writers Authors Course: Writers and authors, of course, craft compelling works forreaders to enjoy, while literary critics analyze and review books to provide.
Options Include Careers: Other options include careers in academia, where professors and researchers frequently engage with texts to educate and innovate in their fields.
Lawyersand Paralegals: Lawyersand paralegals also have careers deeply intertwined with reading, as they analyzelegal documents, contracts, and case studies.
